title: Aamir Khan Says a Film Flopping Feels Like 'Losing a Child' — and His Son's Ek Din Just Broke His Heart
excerpt: The actor who made NRIs cry with 3 Idiots now admits he doesn't understand how to market films anymore. His son Junaid says he's learned to stop asking Dad for help.
body:
For a generation of Indians who grew up abroad, Aamir Khan was the reason you dragged your non-Indian college roommate to a Bollywood film. 3 Idiots was the gateway drug. PK sealed the deal. Dangal was the one you watched with your parents and nobody had to explain the jokes.

So when Aamir Khan tells Zee Music Company that a film flopping sends him into a months-long depression — comparing it to "losing a child" — it lands differently than it would from most actors. This isn't somebody who phones it in. This is the man who gained 25 kilograms for a role and then lost it all again because the timeline demanded it.

The occasion for his confession: Ek Din, a romantic drama he produced for his son Junaid Khan and co-starring Sai Pallavi. The film opened to roughly ₹1 crore on Day 1 and crawled to ₹4.30 crore net across 11 days in India — ₹5.44 crore globally. Against a reported budget of ₹25 crore, that's a loss north of ₹20 crore.

The numbers tell only half the story.

This was Junaid's second theatrical miss after Loveyapa, which managed ₹7.69 crore. Two flops in a row for a nepo kid — the internet had takes ready before the opening weekend was over. But Aamir's response was disarmingly raw. "I tend to feel depressed for two to three months after a film does not perform well," he said. "A film is akin to your child, and its rejection can be extremely painful. I believe it's vital to grieve these losses."

He also dropped a quieter bombshell: he no longer understands film marketing. The actor who once ran legendarily meticulous promotional campaigns — the Ghajini haircut trend, the PK poster controversy, the Dangal real-wrestling tours — now admits he's lost at sea. "I don't know what's happening with marketing," he told Zee Music. "It used to be so simple — a few TV spots, some press. Now it's fragmented across so many platforms, I can't even keep up."

The Father-Son Fault Line

Junaid Khan, for his part, has drawn a fascinating line. Speaking to journalist Vickey Lalwani, he said he's resolved not to ask his father for feedback on future projects. "I learned my lesson with Ek Din. I initially considered asking for Dad's opinion, and when he showed enthusiasm, it led to him producing it. While I appreciate his support, I realize that this could slow my own progress."

That's a remarkably self-aware thing for a 31-year-old in Bollywood to say publicly. It's also a quiet indictment of how the Khan production machine, for all its good intentions, can become a liability — the hype of an Aamir Khan production raises expectations to a height that a modest romantic drama simply cannot meet.

What NRIs Are Really Watching

Here's the uncomfortable truth for Bollywood's traditional model: the diaspora audience that once reliably filled Thursday-night premieres in Edison, Fremont, and Hounslow has options now. Korean dramas are on Netflix. RRR proved that South Indian cinema doesn't need a Hindi dub to sell out American theaters. And Junaid Khan, talented though he may be, doesn't yet have the name recognition to compete for NRI eyeballs.

Ek Din earned just over ₹1 crore overseas across its entire run — a number that wouldn't even register in the old Aamir Khan playbook, where Dangal alone made ₹374 crore in China.

The critical reception was actually positive. Reviewers praised the performances and Sunil Pandey's direction. But critical acclaim without commercial traction is Bollywood's cruelest paradox — especially for an actor's son whose every ticket sold gets measured against his father's filmography.

What Comes Next

Aamir Khan is currently in production on a partition-era cricket biopic with Farhan Akhtar and developing the 3 Idiots sequel with the original cast and Rajkumar Hirani. Both projects will arrive with built-in NRI nostalgia and global distribution infrastructure that Ek Din never had.

For Junaid, the path forward is harder and arguably more interesting. He's choosing to step out of his father's shadow — publicly, deliberately, and at a moment when the industry is watching to see if he'll lean into the family name or try to build something of his own.

Aamir, meanwhile, continues to grieve the way he always has: honestly, and with the kind of emotional transparency that made NRIs fall in love with him in the first place.
